concept.name: Backup to the edge of the creek
concept.definition: The Wyckoff event (BU) in which price pulls back toward the resistance it just crossed with a sign of strength, combining profit-taking with a test for remaining supply around the old resistance area. The term comes from Robert Evans's creek metaphor and precedes a more substantial markup.
concept.intuition: After leaping over the creek of resistance, the market walks back to the water's edge to make sure the far bank is solid before marching on.
concept.mechanics: Following a jump across the creek (SOS through resistance), price retreats on narrowing spread and lower volume toward the breakout area; a successful back-up holds above or near the old resistance and is treated as an entry or add-on point. A back-up can take several forms, from a simple pullback to a small new trading range at a higher level.
concept.failure_modes: A back-up that sinks decisively back into the trading range on expanding volume shows the breakout lacked sponsorship and often precedes a return to the range or a breakdown.
concept.misconceptions: A back-up is not merely any dip after a breakout; the Wyckoff reading depends on diminished volume and spread during the retreat and on the creek level acting as support.
concept.example: A stock jumps from 100 to 110 through range resistance, then drifts back to 104 on drying volume over five sessions; the analyst treats the drift as a back-up and adds to the long.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
